statement: An observational error (or measurement error) $e$ is the difference between a measured value $y$ of a quantity and its unknown true value $x$, defined by $e = y - x$. Under the common additive statistical measurement model, the measured value is modeled as $y = x + e_{\text{sys}} + e_{\text{rand}}$, where the total observational error $e = e_{\text{sys}} + e_{\text{rand}}$ is composed of an additive systematic error component $e_{\text{sys}}$ (which consistently acts in the same direction across repeated measurements under identical conditions) and an additive random error component $e_{\text{rand}}$ (which varies unpredictably from observation to observation).

symbols.meaning: unknown true value of the quantity

properties.property: The effect of random error can be reduced by averaging repeated measurements, whereas repeated identical measurements do not reduce systematic error.
properties.why: Random errors fluctuate unpredictably about a mean, whereas systematic errors arise from causes that consistently act in the same way and alter results in the same direction.

properties.property: Random errors are uncorrelated between measurements and can be quantified by calculating the standard deviation of a large set of repeated measurements.
properties.why: Unpredictable fluctuations create a distribution of inconsistent readings whose spread directly reflects the precision of the instrument.

properties.property: Systematic error (statistical bias) is caused by repeatable processes inherent to the system and can be eliminated or corrected if its cause is identified.
properties.why: Systematic errors stem from determinate mechanisms such as imperfect calibration (zero error), environmental interference, or incorrect theoretical models.

properties.property: When two or more measurements or instruments are combined, the resulting error depends on the statistical characteristics of each measurement and any statistical correlation between them.
properties.why: Errors propagate through combinations in accordance with their individual variances and mutual covariance.

properties.property: Stochastic errors tend to be normally distributed when the error is the sum of many independent random errors.
properties.why: The central limit theorem dictates that the sum of multiple independent random error sources converges toward a normal distribution.

assumptions.assumption: Measurement error decomposes additively into a systematic error component and a random error component.
assumptions.breaks_when: Errors interact non-additively or cannot be cleanly separated into distinct random and systematic parts, such as complex calibration uncertainties.

assumptions.assumption: Random errors are statistically uncorrelated between successive repeated measurements.
assumptions.breaks_when: Interference from surroundings or measurement latency introduces serial correlation across observations.

assumptions.assumption: Systematic error remains constant or predictable across repeated measurements under the same conditions.
assumptions.breaks_when: Instrument drift occurs over the course of the experiment, such as an instrument warming up and shifting its baseline over time.

failure_modes.signature: Measurements display high precision (low variance) but cluster around an incorrect value, with repeated measurement averaging failing to reduce the offset.
failure_modes.cause: Imperfect calibration of the measuring instrument (such as non-zero initial reading / zero error), unmodeled environmental effects (e.g., thermal expansion), or flawed observation protocols.

failure_modes.signature: Measurements of a constant quantity show a time-dependent trend or unidirectional shift rather than stationary random fluctuation about a constant mean.
failure_modes.cause: Physical changes in the apparatus during the experiment, such as thermal warming or component aging altering the baseline zero reading.

failure_modes.signature: Estimated regression coefficients are biased and standard hypothesis tests are rendered invalid.
failure_modes.cause: Measurement error is present in one or more independent (explanatory) variables in a regression analysis.

instantiation.why_here: In agrios_ws, the obstaclelayer component processes sensor observations to detect and represent obstacles in the environment. The measurement model provides the mathematical framework relating observed sensor data to the true physical state by modeling additive systematic bias and random noise. The component's obstacle tracking and mapping algorithms require this result to interpret and handle observational errors in incoming measurements.
